newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico elections are referendum on Zedillo - PRI.
newsitem.headline: Mexico elections are referendum on Zedillo - PRI.

text.p: Mexico's July congressional and gubernatorial elections are a kind of referendum on President Ernesto Zedillo's policies, the number two of the ruling Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI) said in an interview published Monday.

"The elections are practically that (a referendum). When a citizen casts his vote, he is making a judgement on the municipal, state or federal government and on how government policy has affected him," PRI secretary-general Juan S. Millan told the daily Reforma.

Zedillo has begun campaigning aggressively on behalf of the PRI for the July vote, sparking protests from the opposition who complain that he had promised to stay above party politics to promote greater democracy in Mexico.

Some political analysts say that Zedillo's decision to join the fray is the result of pressure from party hardliners who have told him that his reforms have hurt the PRI and that the time has come to stop giving ground to the opposition.

Millan, who is closely identified with the old-guard Workers Sector of the PRI, told Reforma that if the PRI were to lose its majority in the lower house of Congress for the first time ever it would be "as if the population were reproaching presidential decisions".
Reforma also published Monday an opinion poll showing that 63 percent of Mexicans rejected Zedillo's decision to campaign openly on behalf of the PRI.
Thirty-one percent said the president was right to do so and six percent were undecided.
The same Reforma survey, answered by phone by 800 respondents in 25 states between April 25-26, also gave Zedillo a 50 percent approval rating, with 39 percent disapproving and 11 percent unsure.
Zedillo's new campaign style has also proved unpopular with some political analysts.
Lorenzo Meyer, a professor at the Colegio de Mexico, said Zedillo's original promise of a "sane distance" from his party had been replaced by an "insane closeness".
That frank comment cost Meyer his job as a Monday panelist on a popular Mexico City radio show, Para Empezar, the news magazine Proceso reported Monday.

Proceso alleged that the Interior Ministry or the presidency had lobbied the radio to stop using Meyer after his anti-Zedillo comments. Governmment officials were not immediately available for comment on the issue.
